text: Six more, a sentence or two each. Name resources with plural nouns for collections and IDs for members: articles, article forty-two, its comments beneath it. No verbs in paths: the method is the verb. An action like publish becomes a state change: patch the status to published. So the blog is two collections: GET and POST on articles, GET, PATCH and DELETE on one article, GET and POST on its comments. Filters go in the query string, and a create answers two oh one, with a Location header pointing at the new article. Version an API to protect clients from breaking changes, like removing a field or changing its type. A version in the path, slash v one, is the most visible and the pragmatic default. Adding an optional field needs no new version. Errors get the right status code and a consistent body: a stable code a client can branch on, a message for a person, and details per field. Never a stack trace. Hate-ee-oss, hypermedia as the engine of application state, means responses carry links to what the client can do next. Rest as first defined requires it; in practice most APIs skip it, though a link to the next page is common. Content negotiation lets one URL serve several representations: Accept says what the client can take, and Content-Type what it got. Encoding works the same way: ask for gzip, and this page of twenty articles arrives at about a sixth of its size. Behind every one of these endpoints, the data has to live somewhere. Next: databases.
